title: New insights on interpersonal violence in the Late Pleistocene based on the Nile valley cemetery of Jebel Sahaba

nodes.title: New insights on interpersonal violence in the Late Pleistocene based on the Nile valley cemetery of Jebel Sahaba (intro)
nodes.summary: Reanalysis of the Jebel Sahaba cemetery (Nile Valley, ~13.4 ka, 61 individuals) using microscopic lesion analysis. Over 100 healed and unhealed lesions were found, including embedded lithics, mostly from projectile weapons. Repeated interpersonal violence is confirmed, with a quarter of victims showing both healed and unhealed trauma, rejecting a single-event warfare interpretation. Context covers Late Pleistocene climate change, other Nile sites with violence evidence, the Qadan lithic association, and debates over the cemetery's dating, violence, and mortuary practices.

nodes.title: Results
key_items: Reassessment of the evidence of interpersonal violence.
Reassessment of the evidence of interpersonal violence.
nodes.summary: Reassesses the Jebel Sahaba cemetery (Nile Valley, Site 117) skeletal remains, identifying 106 new lesions, including 52 projectile impact marks, and 21 additional individuals with interpersonal trauma; 41 of 61 individuals (67.2%) show healed or unhealed lesions, mostly traumatic, with no sex bias. Healed parry fractures cluster on the ulnae of females; projectile marks concentrate on the lower limbs and pelvis; cranial perforations are mainly in non-adults. Three case studies (JS 13/14, JS 31, JS 44) detail projectile and blunt trauma, drag marks, and embedded lithics. Lithic reassessment identifies 132 artefacts linked to 28 individuals, interpreted as Qadan-industry composite projectiles. Mortality analysis finds no demographic anomaly suggesting a single warfare event, though young children are underrepresented.

nodes.title: Discussion
nodes.summary: The text discusses the Jebel Sahaba cemetery (Late Pleistocene Nile valley), long considered the oldest evidence of organized warfare. Re-examination using macroscopic and microscopic methods distinguishes projectile injuries from cutmarks and taphonomic damage. Most individuals with lesions show trauma, with projectile impacts in 61%, many with embedded lithic artefacts, indicating composite projectile weapons. Healed and unhealed lesions co-occur, showing repeated, non-lethal violence across ages and sexes. Comparisons are made with Nataruk and Wadi Halfa, and the violence is attributed to inter-group raids or ambushes rather than a single mass event or domestic conflict. Climate change and resource competition are proposed as likely drivers.

nodes.title: Conclusions
nodes.summary: Reassessment of the Jebel Sahaba cemetery: direct radiocarbon dates of 13.4-18.2 ka make it the oldest Nile valley cemetery. Analyses of 61 individuals confirm interpersonal, mostly projectile-caused trauma: 26.2% perimortem, 62.3% healed or unhealed, across all ages and sexes including a 4-year-old. Lithics were mostly composite projectile weapon elements. Multiple burials and reuse of the space do not indicate one catastrophic event but recurrent small-scale violence (skirmishes, raids, ambushes) at the end of the Pleistocene, likely driven by climate-related territorial and environmental pressures among semi-sedentary hunter-fisher-gatherer groups.

nodes.summary: Describes the methods for reanalyzing the Jebel Sahaba skeletal collection held at the British Museum: archive provenance, missing individuals, and lithic artefact association; biological sex and age estimation procedures; demographic cohort analysis; and microscopic lesion and projectile impact mark characterization, including taphonomic exclusion and healing criteria.

nodes.summary: This is a reference list (items 1–91) from a 2021 Scientific Reports paper on Nile Valley and Nubian prehistory. It cites works on past climate and the African Humid Period, Late Paleolithic sites such as Jebel Sahaba, Wadi Kubbaniya, and Wadi Halfa, and the origins and evidence of prehistoric warfare and interpersonal violence. It also covers trauma and projectile-injury analysis, paleodemography, skeletal sex and age estimation, taphonomy, and tooth wear.
